title: Ceebu Yapp
localName: Ceebu yapp — riz à la viande sénégalais
author: Cuisine Teranga
desc: An easy ceebu yapp published under a site byline — the simplest documented route into the meat thieb.
longDesc: The most approachable of the documented ceebu yapp recipes, published under a site name rather than a personal byline and flagged as such. It follows the same architecture as every Senegalese rice-and-meat dish — brown the meat, caramelise the onions hard for colour, build a broth, finish the rice in it — with fewer components than the household versions and no separate onion sauce to make alongside.
ingredients: // The source's quantities are recorded in the note; several are absent
Meat, cut into pieces — beef or lamb
steps: Brown the meat in hot oil until well coloured.
Add the sliced onions and diced bell pepper and caramelise them well.
Add the garlic and the tomato paste and cook it down.
Add the water, the bay leaf, the chilli and the bouillon, and bring to the boil.
Simmer until the meat is tender.
Add the carrot and cook until done, then remove the vegetables and meat and keep them warm.
Add the washed rice to the broth, with the liquid just covering the grain.
Cover and cook until the rice is tender and the broth absorbed.
Serve the rice with the meat and vegetables on top.
chefTips: This is the one to start with if you have not made a Senegalese rice dish before — same technique, fewer moving parts than the household versions.
Caramelise the onions properly even here. It is the step that makes a thieb taste Senegalese rather than merely like rice with meat.
Broth just covering the rice, as in every version of this dish.
Remove the meat and vegetables before the rice goes in. They will overcook otherwise and you want them intact on the platter.
Published under a site byline rather than a person's name, which this collection flags. For a named-author version of the same dish, SEN007 and SEN008 are both by a Senegalese cook.
Tomato paste here, unlike the browned-onion-only household versions. It is a legitimate variation and it gives colour more easily.
Once you can make this, the step up to a full ceebu jen is mostly about the fish and the fermented seasonings.
commonMistakes: Skipping the caramelising because the tomato paste provides colour.
Leaving the meat in through the rice stage.
Boiling rather than simmering the meat.
sources: Adapted from 'Ceebu Yapp facile: Riz à la viande sénégalais', Cuisine Teranga. BYLINE: the SITE NAME 'Cuisine Teranga', not a person — flagged, as this collection flags every site-name byline.

A SOURCING LIMIT, stated plainly: the quantities recovered from this page were incomplete, and the method above follows the architecture the source describes rather than a fully transcribed ingredient list. No quantity has been invented; the ingredient list carries no amounts because the recovered source text carried none reliably. The five servings is editorial.

WHY IT IS PUBLISHED: ceebu yapp is a major Senegalese dish and the best French-language full recipes for it sit on travel and tourism portals, which this collection excludes. Among the sources that pass the bar, this is the most straightforward treatment. A reader who wants quantities should use SEN008, which is by a named Senegalese cook and fully specified, and this entry's value is as the simplest statement of the dish's shape.

A RELATED PRINTING, recorded for completeness and NOT used as the basis of this entry: whats4eats carries a ceebu yapp variation which the research round flagged as CONTAINING A MISPRINT. It is not reproduced here.

SOURCES EXCLUDED FOR THIS DISH, recorded so the gap is understood rather than mistaken for thin research: au-senegal.com, visitezlesenegal.com, my-gambia.com, fairmoove.fr, trek.zone, tripbase.com and mustseespots.com all carry ceebu yapp material and are all travel or tourism publishers, which this collection does not cite for recipes. au-senegal.com is a country portal published by Agence Pointcom rather than a tour operator, but it carries hotel and tourism listings and prints no personal byline on its recipe pages, where the author metadata reads 'le cœur du Sénégal' — the site's own tagline.
ON THE SPELLING: ceebu yapp in Wolof orthography, thiebou yapp or thiébou yap in the French-influenced spelling. The same dish throughout.
reheating: Steam the rice; warm the meat gently.
healthBenefits: A one-pot meal with its vegetables built in.
culturalNote: Teranga is the Wolof word for hospitality and it is the word Senegal uses about itself, so a site called Cuisine Teranga publishing the easy version of the meat thieb is about right — the dish you make for whoever turns up.
